newsitem.title: USA: FULL TEXT - Motorola Q3 sales, net fall.
newsitem.headline: FULL TEXT - Motorola Q3 sales, net fall.

text.p: Motorola Inc said Monday its 1996 third quarter earnings fell from year ago levels due to a recession in the semiconductor industry, competitive pressures and continuing price declines in cellular telephone, paging and modem businesses. Results also reflect the impact of weaker sales and order patterns on related component products such as rechargeable batteries, as additional factors.

Motorola reported 1996 third quarter earnings fell to $0.34 a share on a diluted basis, down from $0.81 earned in the same period a year ago. According to First Call, analysts consensus third quarter estimate was $0.35 a share.
The full text of Motorola's news release follows.
SCHAUMBURG, Ill.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 7, 1996--Motorola, Inc. today reported lower sales and earnings in the third quarter of l996.
Third quarter sales declined 5 percent to $6.5 billion from $6.9 billion in the third quarter of 1995. In the first nine months, sales were $20.3 billion, up 3 percent from $19.7 billion a year ago.

Third quarter earnings were $206 million, compared with $496 million in the third quarter of 1995. Fully diluted earnings per common and common equivalent share were 34 cents, down from 81 cents in the third quarter of 1995. Earnings in the first nine months were $916 million, compared with $1.35 billion in 1995. Fully diluted earnings per common and common equivalent share were $1.51, compared with $2.21 a year earlier.

Net margin on sales was 3.2 percent in the third quarter, compared with 7.2 percent a year ago, while in the first nine months, net margin was 4.5 percent compared with 6.8 percent in the year-earlier period.

Christopher Galvin, president and chief operating officer, attributed the decline in third-quarter earnings primarily to the recession in the semiconductor industry and also cited competitive pressures and continuing price declines in cellular telephone, paging, and modem businesses, and the impact of weaker sales and order patterns on related component products such as rechargeable batteries, as additional factors. These issues were noted in the Company's preliminary third-quarter announcement in September 1996. In addition, the earnings comparison is even less favorable due to a substantial net gain on the sale of certain assets in the third quarter of 1995, which favorably affected the results in the year-ago quarter.

"Because of the continuing weakness in some of our businesses, primarily the Semiconductor Products Sector, the Company is expanding cost-cutting actions already under way, including manufacturing and work force adjustments. Specific actions are expected to be finalized during the fourth quarter and will have an adverse effect on fourth-quarter earnings."
Galvin reviewed the following third-quarter results of Motorola's major operations, compared with the year-earlier quarter:
General Systems Sector
Segment sales declined 2 percent to $2.6 billion. Orders increased 13 percent and operating profits were lower.

Cellular Subscriber Group (CSG) orders increased while sales were lower as the effect of higher unit shipments was offset by declining prices. Cellular Infrastructure Group (CIG) sales were higher and orders increased significantly, due to strength in international markets. Computer Group sales were lower but orders increased.

Motorola introduced the StarTAC(TM) 6000 phone. It is a mid-tier featured and lower priced addition to its wearable phone family. CSG also announced that the MicroTAC(R) SC-720 phone for Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) networks is commercially available.

Other new phones announced include the Micro Digital(TM) M75 phone, the lightest available for Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) networks in North America. This dual-mode phone supports Short Message Services, a pager-like feature with a scrolling display. The phone can be used on TDMA digital systems or AMPS analog systems. Also introduced was an additional new Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) digital product for the 1.9 gigahertz U.S. Personal Communication Service (PCS) market.

The group also made production shipments of the 900 megahertz MicroTAC(R) International 8700 GSM phone in Europe and Asia. It provides more talk and standby times than most currently available GSM units on the market today.
CIG received a $53 million supply contract with Bell Atlantic NYNEX Mobile, which includes CDMA deployment in Phoenix, Ariz., and Charlotte, N.C.

The first calls were made by Fujian PTA in China on a Motorola CDMA WiLL(R) system, which provides wireless local loop service. The group also received major contracts to expand the analog cellular systems in Jiangsu and Shanghai, China, and contracts to deploy GSM digital cellular networks in Karnataka and Punjab in India.

Telefonica del Peru successfully completed its first CDMA phone call using Motorola equipment. The system is on target for commercial service in the fourth quarter. TELCEL became the first cellular operator in Venezuela to offer CDMA digital technology to existing customers when it launched a six-month trial of Motorola's CDMA equipment.
T-Mobil, located in Germany, announced plans to trial a Motorola CDMA system. Contracts for Digital Communications System (DCS) 1800 networks were received in Norway and the Ukraine.

The Computer Group introduced its new StarMax(TM) family of computers, which use PowerPC(TM) 603e and 604e microprocessors and are compatible with the Mac(R) OS operating system. The group also unveiled its PowerStack(TM) II series of PowerPC-based computers optimized for Microsoft's Windows NT(R) operating system.
Semiconductor Products Sector
Segment sales declined 19 percent to $1.8 billion. Orders were 33 percent lower and operating profits were significantly lower, essentially at break-even.
Orders were lower in all geographic regions versus a year ago. Among major market segments, only automotive posted a gain in orders. Distributor orders were lower.
All of the sector's technology groups experienced weaker orders. All product categories experienced weaker orders except sensor products, where orders were higher.

Design wins for embedded control applications continued to expand. The PowerPC(TM)-based MPC801 processor was selected by Mitsubishi for its DiamondWeb(TM) television set that will enable viewers to access the Internet. Bay Networks chose PowerPC-based communication processors for next-generation network management modules. Samsung selected a Motorola 16-bit microcontroller for hard disk drives.

The sector announced availability of three PowerPC 604e microprocessors with clock speeds up to 200 megahertz. Initiatives to speed time-to-market for customers included the MCUs-In-A-Day(SM) program, offering North American customers one-day shipment of one-time programmable microcontrollers.

The sector continued to take cost-cutting steps to address the slowdown in the global semiconductor industry. In September, the sector began phasing down pilot production at the COM 1 start-up facility in Phoenix and on one of the wafer production lines in East Kilbride, Scotland.
Messaging, Information and Media Sector

Segment sales rose 8 percent to $1.0 billion, while orders declined 2 percent. Operating profits were lower largely because of the substantial net gain recorded in the year-ago quarter from the sale of an investment.

Sales were higher in all business units. Paging orders were flat with a year ago, as lower orders in Asia, particularly China, offset increased orders in Pan America and Europe. Paging's growth rates were adversely affected by competitive pricing pressures for pagers, as well as a reduction of inventory in Asian distribution channels. Orders were also lower in the Information Systems Group, reflecting a continuation of a very competitive pricing environment for modems.
The Tango(R) Lite two-way messaging device was announced. It will operate on the ReFLEX(TM) protocol. To date, more than 100 carriers have adopted Motorola's FLEX(TM) family of technologies.
The group also announced the PageWriter(TM) pocket message center. Based on Motorola's Memos(TM) software, it features a keyboard and graphical interface.

Time Warner launched the first city-wide commercial deployment of high-speed Internet access service on its upgraded hybrid fiber coax cable network in Akron, Ohio. The services are based on Motorola's high-speed CyberSURFR(TM) cable modems and data communications infrastructure equipment, part of the CableComm family of products.
The Wireless Data Group introduced the Personal Messenger(TM) 100C Wireless Modem Card for wide-area communications on the Cellular Digital Packet Data network.

The Lexicus Division announced that its QuickPrint(R) handwriting recognition software and CrystalTalk(TM) speech recognition software were ported to the OS-9(R) Real-Time Operating System from Microware Systems Corporation.
Land Mobile Products Sector
Segment sales rose 2 percent to $929 million, orders increased 18 percent, and operating profits were higher.

Nextel Communications, Inc. placed orders for more than $200 million in iDEN(TM) infrastructure and subscriber equipment as part of the continued roll-out of its nationwide network in the U.S. Motorola announced two new digital handsets designed to operate on the integrated Dispatch Enhanced Network. One portable is a compact handset that integrates full-duplex telephone interconnect and alphanumeric paging service; while another portable has a rugged design for extreme environmental conditions, which integrates telephone interconnect, instant group conferencing and wireless intercom, along with alphanumeric paging.

Two key contracts in the public safety sector were awarded by the City of Boston and the State of New Hampshire. The sector introduced its first two-way radio system that is compliant with the Association of Public Safety Communications International Project 25 digital standard.

Major orders for trunking systems were received in the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy and Angola. An order for infrastructure that complies with the new Trans European Trunked Radio (TETRA) standard was received from Gardermo Airport in Norway.

At the 1996 Centennial Olympic Games in Atlanta, Motorola's Astro(R) Smartzone(R) system handled more than 4 million two-way radio calls, and 99.99% of all calls were completed without a delay. The iDEN systems operating in the Atlanta area supported the 1,400 iDEN radios used in the Olympics' transportation system and approximately 7 million additional calls with comparable call completion performance.
Automotive, Energy and Controls Group (AECG).

Group sales were 13 percent lower, orders declined 12 percent, and operating profits were lower. The group's results are reported as part of the "Other Products" segment. Pricing pressures and reduced demand for components and rechargeable batteries for cellular telephones were the primary factors in the Group's performance versus a year ago. The Automotive and Industrial Electronics portion of the Group's business reported increased sales, orders and profits.
AECG has implemented a series of cost cutting measures and in September announced a voluntary severance program for its component businesses and headquarters employees.

The Automotive and Industrial Electronics Group (AIEG) was awarded body electronics business by a major U.S. automotive manufacturer for its model year 2000 luxury vehicle. AIEG's Angers, France, facility received a national quality award from the Mouvement Francais pour la Qualite, the French equivalent of the Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award.
The Component Products Group secured new external customers for components for cordless telephone, paging, computer peripherals and CDMA cellular telephone protocols.
Space and Systems Technology Group (SSTG)
Group sales were 3 percent higher. Orders were 437 percent higher, and the group recorded an operating profit, compared with a loss a year ago.

The significant increase in orders reflects recognition of order bookings that had been delayed pending completion by Iridium L.L.C., of a $750 million short-term credit facility that enabled it to continue to make contractual payments to Motorola. Development of the IRIDIUM global telecommunications system continued on schedule, as Motorola met all contractual milestones during the quarter.

Selling, general and administrative expenses decreased to 16 percent of sales from 17 percent of sales a year ago, as management, in anticipation of continuing pressure on gross margins, maintained its focus during the third quarter of 1996 on controlling these costs.
The tax rate for the quarter was 35 percent compared with 37 percent in the third quarter of 1995 and 36 percent for the full year 1995.
Review and Outlook

Gary Tooker, vice chairman and chief executive officer, said that because of current conditions, Motorola's businesses are continuing to take actions to reduce operating expenses, as well as to defer capital expenditures, which are expected to be about $1.1 billion lower than in 1995. "At the same time," he said, "Motorola continues to invest in programs that are critical to the Company's long-term future."

He said the start of the satellite deployment phase of the IRIDIUM program will result in much higher expenses being reported by Iridium L.L.C., as planned, of which approximately 25 percent are included in Motorola's financial results.

These increased expenses are largely due to satellite depreciation before the system enters commercial service in late 1998. In addition, expenses in the flat-panel display business will increase significantly in 1997. These expenses will have an impact on profitability in 1997.

"We expect a modest recovery in the semiconductor industry in 1997," Tooker said. "As was the case in recoveries from previous industry recessions, the improvement in sales and profitability will be gradual at first, as the industry returns to sustainable growth," he said.

Looking to the longer-term future, Tooker said, "Growth opportunities in existing communications and semiconductor businesses are abundant. In addition, transitions to new technologies are taking place that should have a major positive impact on Motorola's future. These include significant build-out and loading of PCS systems in the U.S., full commercialization of CDMA, two-way paging and voice paging, the commercialization of the IRIDIUM(R) system, and the expansion of opportunities in iDEN(TM) systems, CableComm and Wireless Local Loop."
